title: Analytical insights into the transient climate response
abstract: The temperature in the transient climate response is lower than the equilibrium temperature for the same amount of forcing. The degree of disequilibrium is not constant in time and depends on various climate parameters. We derive intuition for this by solving the heat equation with a surface temperature feedback for linearly increasing forcing. The surface temperature initially evolves at a slower rate than the corresponding steady state (SS) temperature and it accelerates until quasi-steady state (QSS), when the SS and QSS temperatures evolve in parallel with a constant offset. The offset depends on the rate of forcing and total heat capacity of the system divided by the square of the climate feedback. The timescale over which the climate system approaches QSS depends also on the effective ocean mixing and is order of thousands of years. Over societally relevant timescales (around 100 years), the top-of-atmosphere energy imbalance increases, and the actual temperature moves farther from the steady-state temperature expected for the same forcing.
problem: The paper addresses the lack of a physically transparent analytical framework for interpreting the transient climate response, noting that parameters in commonly used two-box models have unclear physical interpretations and lack standard diagnostic procedures from more complex simulations.
method: This paper proposes an analytical solution to the heat equation, with surface temperature feedback and energy-conserving boundary conditions, to describe the transient climate response to linearly increasing forcing and provide insights into the top-of-atmosphere energy imbalance.
task: The task is to provide an analytical framework for interpreting the transient climate response by solving a diffusive ocean heat equation with a surface temperature feedback under linearly increasing forcing.
innovation: This paper presents an analytical solution to the heat equation for linearly increasing forcing, providing a simple, physically transparent framework to interpret the temporal evolution of the transient climate response and its departure from equilibrium.

K is estimated from eq. 16 and y from eq. B6. The estimates of K and y depend on the assumption for total domain depth L = 2600m. To estimate y, we also suppose a ratio between the upper (C1) and deep layer (C2) heat capacities k = C1/C2 = 0.1. dT is the rate of temperature change, dTss is the rate of the corresponding temperature at flux equilibrium, dN is the rate of change of TOA imbalance, dF is the rate of forcing. The ratios of derivatives are based on linear regressions computed over the full length (150 years).
